o: Each chocolate type sits at an index with a price; one operation (cost x) rotates all types forward by one. To collect type i we can buy it at whatever rotation t puts a cheap price there, paying nums[(i−t) mod n] plus t·x accumulated. In Example 1 buying all three at price 1 requires two rotations: 1+5+1+5+1 = 13. In Example 2 rotation is too expensive (x=4), so we pay 1+2+3 = 6. Since rotating n times returns to the start, only t = 0..n−1 matters, and n ≤ 1000 permits O(n²).
k: Only the number of rotations t (0..n−1) matters; after t rotations type i costs nums[(i−t) mod n].
Answer = min over t of (t·x + Σᵢ min over t'≤t of nums[(i−t') mod n]).
Each type can be minimized independently given a shared rotation count.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate rotation count with running minima
a.i: Keep cur[i] = cheapest price seen for type i among rotations 0..t. After each additional rotation update cur with the newly available prices and evaluate total + t·x.
s: Initialize cur = nums, ans = sum(nums) (zero rotations).
For t = 1..n−1: cur[i] = min(cur[i], nums[(i−t) mod n]).
Candidate answer: sum(cur) + t·x; take the minimum.
a.t: O(n²) — n rotation counts, each updating n entries.

a.i: Same idea written differently: physically rotate a copy of the array each step and merge elementwise minima. Identical complexity but often clearer to reason about.
s: best = copy of nums; ans = sum(best).
For t in 1..n−1: rotate nums right by t, best = elementwise min(best, rotated).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minCost(self, nums: List[int], x: int) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        best = nums[:]
        ans = sum(best)
        rot = nums[:]
        for t in range(1, n):
            rot = rot[-1:] + rot[:-1]
            best = [min(b, r) for b, r in zip(best, rot)]
            ans = min(ans, sum(best) + t * x)
        return ans

w: Both approaches are equivalent; pick whichever reads better to you. Watch 64-bit sums (values up to 1e9, n up to 1000 ⇒ totals near 1e12). Common pitfall: trying more than n−1 rotations — they cycle back and can't help. Follow-up: for large n, per-type costs can be minimized with sparse-table RMQ over the doubled array in O(n log n).
